text: You've gotten really comfortable with pandas over the last several chapters, but pandas has a real limit: it only works on data that fits in one machine's memory. This lesson is where that limit stops being theoretical and PySpark enters the picture.

A single month of NYC Taxi trip records is already millions of rows, and a real production dataset is often years of that — at some point it just won't fit on one machine. Spark's whole job is splitting that work across multiple machines or cores, and PySpark is Python's way of talking to it.

Every single PySpark script starts the same way: build a SparkSession. appName just labels the job for Spark's own logs, and getOrCreate reuses an existing session instead of starting a redundant second one. Everything else you do flows through this one spark object.

Here we read the same real NYC Taxi dataset you'll use throughout this chapter — one real month of yellow cab trips with columns like VendorID, trip distance, and fare amount. printSchema is basically PySpark's version of pandas' dtypes: a quick first look before touching anything.

Here's the concept that trips people up at first: filter and groupBy don't actually do anything when you call them — Spark just records what you asked for. That's a transformation. It's only when you call an action, like show, count, or collect, that Spark actually reads the data and runs the whole chain. This lazy evaluation lets Spark plan an efficient execution instead of running line by line like pandas does.

Once you can explain the difference between a transformation and an action without looking it up, you're ready for Lesson 45, where we bring in a second real file — the taxi zone lookup table — and start transforming data with select, filter, and withColumn.
